George I. The first Hanoverian King of Great Britain and Ireland, reigning from 1714 until his death in 1727. A German-born prince who spoke little English and showed minimal interest in British affairs, his reign marked a crucial transition toward constitutional monarchy and parliamentary supremacy, as power gradually shifted from the crown to the Prime Minister.

George I was born George Louis in Hanover in 1660. He became king of Britain through the Act of Settlement of 1701, which barred Catholic heirs and chose him as the nearest Protestant relative. He was aged fifty-four when he ascended the British throne, making him the oldest first-time reigning monarch in English history to that point. He spoke minimal English, relied on German and French, and maintained strong ties to Hanover, often visiting his German principality and delegating British governance to ministers.

His court became known for using German and Hanover customs, and English nobles resented his preference for German courtiers and his apparent indifference to British affairs. He relied heavily on Robert Walpole, who became the first Prime Minister and skillfully managed both the king and Parliament through the monarch's disinterest. Walpole's influence grew because George I delegated power so thoroughly, establishing the precedent of the Prime Minister as the chief executive subordinate to the monarch. His reign solidified parliamentary control over taxation, legislation, and foreign policy, transforming the monarchy from an active decision-maker to a figurehead. He never learned to trust British nobles or institutions, surrounding himself with a small German court clique and maintaining distance from London society. He faced political instability early in his reign, including the Jacobite rising of 1715 among Scottish and Irish supporters of the deposed Stuart line. His distance from governance paradoxically strengthened constitutional development, as Parliament flourished in the power vacuum he left.
